 The Invisible Thread 
 1 Sergeant Gaba Alatak said he needed four police officers, but I was the fifth wheel. He didn’t put it that way, but as soon as we boarded the cruise ship Dreamcaster, I had the feeling I would soon be redundant. The captain of the ship had called for assistance when a group of passengers had become what he described as rowdy. The captain’s thick Texan accent and peculiar American words had confounded Gaba for a moment. And, while I do enjoy seeing what I might call perplexed Gaba – so different to his usual macho self – I could feel his pain, and when he said he needed a language expert, I volunteered. It was the word expert that did it. The cruise ship was anchored between the villages of Qassiarsuk and Narsarsuaq in Qinngua, the thick finger of water above Tunulliarfik Fjord. With its brilliant white hull and light blue smokestacks, it wasn’t a stretch to think it looked like an iceberg, and I stared at the ship as the pilot set up for landing at Narsarsuaq Airport, on the eastern shore of Qinngua. There were more bergs in the fjord, but Dreamcaster was the biggest. “Local police are already onboard,” Gaba said as we piled into the back of an airport pickup for the short drive down to the beach. “They have the situation contained. They passed up the names of the guests…” Gaba paused to tug a crumpled piece of paper from the chest pocket of his ballistic vest and squinted in the bright light as he read the names aloud. “Alex Waldren, Ray Liddell, Rachael Silk…” Another pause. Gaba looked at me as if Rachael were to be my personal responsibility. I gripped the side of the pickup and nodded as expected. “And Sean Augustus Arnet.” Gaba made a show of looking at the list one more time and then tucked it back into his pocket. The pickup bumped into and out of a line of potholes, drawing a smile from the two officers – Constable Naatat Saarullik and Constable Jaakorpi Taateraaq – sitting closest to the cab, and a cloud of dust and grit caught Gaba by surprise as he took a breath. He leaned over the side of the pickup to spit grit from his mouth and then turned back to the team. We were what I chose to call almost ready for battle. Gaba had insisted on ballistic vests and MP5 submachine guns, along with our service pistols, but no helmets. The captain had described the American guests – aged between twenty-nine and forty-three – as belligerent, another word that confounded Gaba for a second as he searched for the Greenlandic equivalent. It wasn’t that he couldn’t speak English, but the more interesting words taxed him in between, and bumped me up to Special Response Unit status, at least for the duration of the operation. “And there’s our ride,” Gaba said, nodding at a small fibreglass dinghy as the driver slowed the pickup to a stop just above a narrow strip of sandy beach. We climbed over the sides of the pickup and Gaba snapped his fingers at me, and then pointed at the dinghy he had rented for the trip across the fjord to the cruise ship. “Jensen drives,” he said, before turning to Saarullik and telling him he had point once we were aboard the cruise ship, that Taateraaq would bring up the rear, with me and Gaba in the middle. I wanted to check that the locals had the guests in custody, but Gaba bounced that thought out of my head when he said, “Arnet is our priority. His name popped up on a watchlist. Why he thought he could use his real name, I don’t know. But the Americans want him, and I said we could deliver.” “Want him for what?” Saarullik said as we shoved the stern of the boat deeper into the water. “Diamond smuggling,” Gaba said with a grin. “Amongst other things.” He nodded for me to climb in the boat, waited for Saarullik to join me, before holding onto the bow as I prepped the outboard motor. The mountains on either side of the fjord wore a light grey summer coat, having shed the last threads of winter, but the air was still cool, and a light breeze caught the loose strands of my hair. I tucked them behind my ears, pumped fuel from the bladder into the engine, and then fiddled with the choke. I fiddled for longer than Gaba thought necessary, but then he couldn’t know what I was thinking. Aside from the fact that I didn’t want Gaba to ever know what was going on inside my head, the mountains and the fjord and the boat brought back memories of the last time I was in Narsarsuaq, including memories of a brief encounter with Carran Brigham, an interesting Brit from England, and, of course, Constable Innaaq Paniula. I hadn’t thought about him for a long time, but as I lowered the propeller shaft into the water, I couldn’t help but think of what had happened that time I had sprung a winter trap. “Constable?” “Yes,” I said, as Gaba’s voice jogged me back into the moment. “Everything all right?” Everything was all right, and I knew that, had we been alone, I might have told Gaba at least a little of what I was thinking. But the way he called me Jensen and Constable reminded me that we were not alone, and the regular members of the SRU, including Constable Atii Napa, were otherwise engaged. Saarullik and Taateraaq were Gaba’s stand ins – competent but still needing to prove themselves. Proving oneself to Sergeant Gaba Alatak was something many of my male colleagues seemed to spend a lot of time doing, and a quick glance at Saarullik and Taateraaq revealed they were no different. “I’m fine,” I said. “Just got distracted for a moment.” I gestured at the fjord and the mountains as if the stark beauty of Southern Greenland might explain it. The flicker of light in Gaba’s eye when he looked at me suggested he had suddenly remembered some of what had happened in Narsarsuaq, but a curt nod of his shaved and oiled head encouraged me to stop dawdling and start the motor. I pulled the choke lever out a little further, restricting the air intake a little more, clicked the gear into neutral, and yanked the starting handle. “Everybody in,” Gaba shouted as the motor caught the first time. Sure, it looked like a well-maintained outboard motor, but I enjoyed the nods of approval among the men as I – the only girl in the gang – proved I knew what I was doing. Gaba, the last man on the beach, gave the bow one more shove, pushing the dinghy into the fjord, and then climbed over the gunwales. “Go,” he said, before settling on the thwart seat. The wind teased several strands of my hair out of my hairband, and I glanced at Gaba, catching his eye, catching him looking. It was one of those heart-fluttering moments that made my professional and personal relationship with the macho leader of the SRU so interesting. But so long as he and Atii were still trying to make a go of things, I preferred to keep things simple. Yes, I know, lots of thoughts swirling around my head. But as I steered the dinghy into the wind, quartering the shallow waves en route to the cruise ship Dreamcaster, the fresh air helped me focus, and I listened as Gaba briefed us on Sean Augustus Arnet, diamond smuggler, and one of America’s Most Wanted. 
 2 Sean Augustus Arnet. I was going to remember that name. Gaba painted a picture of a man with a bland appearance – white skin, quite pale, thinning brown hair, and pale blue eyes – who chose equally bland clothing, and could blend into a crowd. I found it curious that Gaba was not reading aloud from notes from another crumpled piece of paper he had tucked into his ballistic vest, but briefing us from what he remembered reading in Arnet’s file. Gaba had been quiet on the flight south, from Nuuk to Narsarsuaq, and as I picked a relatively calm course to the cruise ship, I now understood why. “He’s been on the wanted list for over six years,” Gaba said, raising his voice above the thud and thump of the hull as we crested a wave and dropped into the trough on the other side. The fjord was choppier in the middle, and I could see small herds of white horses splashing against the side of Dreamcaster’s hull and frothing up through the metal grille of the platform the crew had set up to receive us. “And was last seen in London…” Gaba paused for effect. “Over four years ago.” Which only made me wonder, what had happened to blow Arnet’s cover on a cruise ship in Greenland? “He must have screwed up,” Saarullik said. He looked around the team, searching for nods of approval, waiting for the nod from Gaba. But Gaba shook his head. “Since making the list,” he said, “Arnet has screwed up only once.” “In London,” Saarullik said. “Aap.” Gaba nodded, and I had to bite my lip to hide my smile when I saw Saarullik’s chest swell as the biggest, baddest, toughest – you name it – sergeant in the whole of Greenland, agreed with him. I might have embellished some of the euphemisms. Euphemism. Good word. But it didn’t matter. Gaba deflated Saarullik a second later. “But he did it on purpose,” he said. “Arnet was reaching out. He wanted a deal.” “He wanted to come in?” Taateraaq said, taking over from Saarullik, although the look on his face suggested he didn’t quite believe it. “That doesn’t make sense.” “It doesn’t,” Gaba said. “But Arnet was, apparently, thinking of his future.” “And a pocketful of diamonds he couldn’t unload,” I said, cutting Gaba off. I wrinkled my nose and gave him an apologetic smile for stealing his thunder. “Sorry. Just guessing.” “Good guess, Constable.” He had to add the constable bit, just to save face. But I let it go, choosing to focus on avoiding a gnarly looking wave that was gathering strength and volume on the port side of the dinghy. Gaba continued without missing a beat. “He had, as Constable Jensen so astutely pointed out, diamonds he couldn’t unload. A deal had gone bad, Scotland Yard got wind of it, and Arnet reached out to try to make the best out of a bad deal. But the English didn’t want to dance, and Arnet slipped away under one of his aliases, leaving over nine hundred thousand British pounds’ worth of two carat diamonds somewhere in London.” Gaba let that thought fester for a moment. He even looked at me, waiting, perhaps, to see if I would comment about the money, or the thought of diamonds. They might once have been a girl’s best friend, but, honestly, my brain is geared differently, and while I could appreciate the sparkle of a diamond ring, or a set of long earrings… Okay, long dangly diamond earrings hanging from my ears might, just might have given me a moment’s pause, but then the gnarly wave arrived, and I was busy trying not to tip Gaba and the SRU into the fjord. “That’s a lot of money,” Saarullik said. “Aap,” Gaba said, rewarding Saarullik with another nod. “But think about this – Arnet walked away from that money. Which means…” “It was pocket money,” I said, apologising for a second time as I beat Gaba to the punchline. I really needed to work on my timing. “Qujanaq, Jensen,” he said, putting me in my place once more by not calling me Petra. “The commissioner spoke with our friends in America this morning,” he said. “They’re dubious about the identity of the passenger called Arnet. But if it is him, then they would appreciate a significant effort to confirm or deny Arnet’s identity, and that’s why we’re here.” “To bring him in?” Taateraaq said. “If necessary.” Gaba was about to nod, but gripped the gunwale instead as I did my best not to soak us all before we arrived. It was touch and go, but with a gentle, if a little desperate, jerk of the tiller, I avoided dumping the wave into the boat, but not without surprising Gaba with a generous spray of saltwater. “Sorry,” I said, my third apology in what felt like as many minutes. Gaba let it go and used a thin fleece beanie he kept in his vest to wipe splashes of chilly Qinngua water from his face. And then we caught the first shout of the crew ready to receive us on the temporary dock tethered to the side of the cruise ship towering above us. The ship’s hull gave us some relief from the wind as we slipped into its shadow, and Gaba finished his briefing before we arrived at the floating dock. “Once Arnet’s identity is confirmed,” he said, “we take him into custody. That’s your job.” He jabbed a thick finger at Saarullik and Taateraaq. “Don’t talk to him.” Gaba jabbed his finger at me and said, “That’s her job. If the Americans let us,” he added with a short but definitive sigh. “Aap, Sergeant,” Saarullik said. Taateraaq nodded in agreement. “Once he’s secured, our job is to babysit him in his cabin while the Americans send a chopper from Kangerlussuaq. Once we give the word, they’ll arrange for personnel on their side to take Arnet off our hands. It could be several hours. During that time, he’s our responsibility. Understood?” Saarullik and Taateraaq nodded that they did, and Gaba turned to catch my eye, to be sure I was on the same page. “I understand,” I said. And, as I steered the dinghy to the dock, I really thought I did. 
 3 Our arrival did not go unnoticed. But the Dreamcaster crew earned Gaba’s respect that day as they kept the passengers entertained and out of our way. Most of them were ashore, hiking from Qassiarsuk to Tasiusaq to visit the Viking settlements, something I had planned to do ever since I discovered that it was the thing to do. But, like many residents of most countries, I never got around to seeing the tourist attractions or historical and cultural heritage sites in my own country. And besides, in Greenland, it wasn’t as if you could just get in a car and drive. Getting around the country required various means of transport, good weather, and a lot of money. Cruise ships provided a more affordable means of seeing Greenland for visitors with relatively deep pockets. But having had one too many experiences on a cruise ship – the exciting and dangerous kind – I didn’t plan on spending any recreation time on a cruise ship any time soon. Meeting Sean Arnet and his companions only compounded such thoughts as I slipped into the middle position allotted me by Gaba and followed Saarullik from deck to deck until we reached Arnet’s cabin. Constable Ortusi Uiluiit greeted Gaba with a firm shake of the hand before talking him through the situation, assuring Gaba that all of Arnet’s party were confined to their cabins, and the extra staff he could see standing two outside each door, were ship security. “And a couple of cooks from below decks,” Uiluiit added with a nod at two lean Asian cooks who could easily have been extras in a martial arts movie. “And you removed all means of self-harm,” Gaba said, framing it somewhere between a statement and a question. “Naturally.” Uiluiit swallowed, and I guessed that he hadn’t made the connection between confining suspects to their cabins and holding them in custody. I caught his eye and gave him a sympathetic smile. To be fair, it was one thing to remember to take a suspect’s belt and shoelaces before placing them in a holding cell, but each cabin no doubt had a small wardrobe of belts and laces, and anything else that might be used to hang themselves from the shower rail, not forgetting the shower curtain for the creatively inclined. “All right,” Gaba said, clicking his fingers at Saarullik and Taateraaq. “Take a cabin each, check they’re still alive, and remove anything harmful.” He clicked his fingers at me and said, “You’ve got Rachael.” “Got it,” I said, and followed Uiluiit’s directions to Rachael Silk’s cabin. The MP5 felt like overkill, but Gaba had insisted. I made the gun safe and cinched the sling tight to my chest before knocking on the door. The ship security guard, plus one musclebound cook, stepped to one side when Rachael called out for me to enter, and I opened the door. Rachael’s perfume – something dark and musky – took me by surprise as I stepped inside the cabin. I pressed my fingers to my nose in an effort not to sneeze, before announcing myself and walking along the short section of hallway with the bathroom on my left. The cabin was L-shaped, and I found Rachael sitting at the end of her bed. She was taller than I imagined, with pale white skin, masculine good looks and a blond pageboy haircut. And, as I did a double take, I realised Rachael was also a man – younger than I had expected, and clearly struggling to come to terms with the situation. “Rachael?” I said. “Yes?” Rachael clearly identified as a woman and I had no intention of treating her otherwise, but her height and build encouraged me to observe a professional distance, just in case she decided to force her way past me and escape the confines of her cabin. Where she would go was a whole other matter, but I kept my distance, nonetheless. “My name is Constable Jensen. I’m with the Greenland police.” “And so is your coworker,” she said, brushing her hair to one side and revealing a bruise on her cheek. I paused for a second as I wondered if Uiluiit had been a little rough when he put Rachael and Arnet’s companions in their cabins, but Rachael caught my eye and smiled. “Don’t worry, honey, it wasn’t your boy who did this. I won’t sue you if that’s what you’re thinking?” “I’m not,” I said, although I could already feel the pinch of my so-called curious frown and could imagine Atii standing in the corner of the cabin and rolling her eyes. It was always this way – curious frown followed by that part of me that always over invested in a case, often teasing at a thread that only got longer and longer the more I pulled on it. But before I could grasp it, Rachael pulled the thread for me. “It was Sean,” she said. “And I want to press charges.” “Sean Arnet?” “Yes,” Rachael said. “Sean Augustus Arnet. Are there any other Seans aboard?” I guessed there would be a few among the predominantly American passenger manifest, but left it at that, not wanting to put words into Rachael’s mouth. I had entered the cabin to check she hadn’t hurt herself, but Sean had apparently beaten me to it. “What’s up, honey? You look a little razzled.” Razzled. Good word, but not one I was familiar with. I took a breath, ready to respond, only to pause as Gaba knocked on the cabin door and then entered, striding into the cabin but stopping short of the living area. “Constable,” he said, after giving Rachael a second look. “A word.” I nodded at Rachael, excused myself, and followed Gaba back into the corridor. He reached out to fiddle with the sling of my MP5 and then grunted when he discovered it didn’t need adjusting. He tucked his hands into his vest and then dipped his head to look me in the eye. “It’s confirmed. We have a positive I.D. on Sean Arnet.” “Right,” I said, followed by a sigh when I understood what that meant. “Then we’re babysitting until the Americans arrive.” “We are,” Gaba said. “Uiluiit has to get back to Narsarsuaq, but we can rotate in shifts. Gaba checked the big watch he had strapped to his wrist and said, “Saarullik and Taateraaq have the first shift. I need to check in with the captain. Leaving you free to explore.” “Explore?” I said. “Aap.” Gaba nodded in the direction of Qassiarsuk and said, “You’ve got four hours. You can take the boat into the village, catch up on a bit of Greenland culture, and still get back in time for a nap before relieving Saarullik and Taateraaq. They’re going to allocate us a cabin – shared, of course.” “Of course,” I said with a shrug. It wouldn’t be the first time. Gaba waited for me to say more, and then followed my gaze as I looked at the door of Rachael’s cabin. “What is it, Constable?” “She was about to say something before you came in,” I said. I tapped my cheek, adding, “And she’s been hit. She said it was Sean.” “Not our problem, Petra.” It was the first time he had used my name since leaving Nuuk, and I guessed it was Gaba’s way of softening the blow when he reminded me of the job at hand, and to not let my curiosity twist the operation into something more complicated. “The Americans are coming,” he said. “Leave it to them.” “We’re just going to ignore it?” “They’re criminals,” Gaba said. “Diamond smugglers. They’ve been on the run for six years or more. Granted, tensions are probably high right now – they’ve been caught, after all. But none of this is our business. We keep them detained, keep them alive, and hand them over as soon as the Americans get here.” Gaba tilted his head to one side to catch my attention as I glanced once more at Rachael’s door. “Constable?” he said. “Do you understand?” “Yes,” I said. “Good.” Gaba clicked his fingers and pointed at my gear. “Give me your gun and vest and take the boat into Qassiarsuk. Do the cultural thing. Be back within a couple of hours, then get another couple of hours of rest. Your shift starts at midnight. Got it?” “Yes,” I said, as I unsnapped the sling from the MP5. “I got it.” But even if I got it, I knew that my mind would twist in one direction and another as I tried to figure out how to get more. Until, of course, something else came along to distract me. 
 4 I couldn’t decide if it was good news that we had a cabin to rest in, or if the fact that we needed one meant the next however many hours we were babysitting Arnet, and his crew, would be the longest hours of my life. Gaba had obviously been talking with Sergeant Duneq back in Nuuk, as he seemed to have pre-empted any union entanglements by splitting up our shift with break periods. It was a new Gaba, and I wondered if he was bucking for a promotion. But when it came to operational procedure, he had a better grip on the proper way to run an operation, including details like suggesting I leave my ballistic vest and submachine gun in his care before joining throngs of tourists in Qassiarsuk. Okay. Maybe Gaba didn’t use the word throngs, but he was still one step ahead of me. As was Constable Uiluiit when I discovered he was waiting for me on the floating dock tethered to Dreamcaster’s port side. “Do you need a ride?” I asked, as I joined him on the dock. The wind and the waves had died down since we boarded the cruise ship, proving once again that it was Greenland, not Gaba, who had the final say in operational matters. In some areas, at least. “Naamik,” Uiluiit said with a shake of his head. He had thick black hair and a curious scar on his right cheek, just below his eye. He caught me looking and said, “Fishhook.” “Really? That must have hurt. Uiluiit laughed and said, “It did.” The thought of meeting Arnet had distracted me on the upper decks, and I had failed to notice that Uiluiit was only a few years older than me. He was shorter, of course, as many of my colleagues were, but with a wiry build and a badly fitting police jacket that threatened to consume him if he didn’t keep his hands in the pockets, pressing it down. Uiluiit also had a gentle laugh, and I tucked my hands into my pockets and leaned against the railing on the dock for what I hoped was an entertaining story from Uiluiit’s childhood. “It happened last year,” he said, nodding as I frowned. “Aap.” Another nod. “I was chasing a small boy along a beach.” “Chasing him?” “Sure,” Uiluiit said, dragging the word out as many Greenlanders do. “Makkoq had been a bad boy. He ran away from his anaana, and his uncle, too.” Uiluiit grinned, and I understood. “You’re the uncle.” “Aap,” he said. “And Makkoq, like his uncle, and his anaana, is cunning.” “I can imagine,” I said, biting my lip as I leaned into the story. “Makkoq is also very small.” Uiluiit demonstrated, holding his hand flat, just below his waist. “Small for his age, but fast. He ran onto the beach…” “Yes,” I said when Uiluiit paused for effect. “He ran towards the drying racks.” “For fish,” I said, nodding as I pictured the spindly wooden structures that could be seen on beaches up and down the Greenland coastline. “Fish, shark, seal…” Uiluiit nodded. “The fishermen dry everything on the racks. Including nets and lines. And Makkoq was just small enough to run under the lines.” “But not you?” I said. “Naamik.” Uiluiit tapped his cheek and said, “I ran through them, got caught on a line, and snagged my cheek.” He shrugged when I wrinkled my nose in sympathy. “Twenty-seven stitches.” I leaned forward for a closer look at Uiluiit’s scar and then shook my head, not quite believing it. The scar wasn’t that long, and I said as much, falling swiftly into the punchline Uiluiit had set up. “Twelve for me,” he said. “And fifteen for Makkoq.” Uiluiit shrugged again and said, “He stopped to laugh. And then, teasing me, he ran circles around the fish rack, and straight into a line the fisherman had stretched between two racks.” Uiluiit raised his arms like a B movie mummy, adding, “He ran straight into it, and he struggled, and it he got snagged.” Uiluiit paused for a breath before he continued. “We spent a few hours together in the hospital, both getting stitches, and then ice cream after that.” “Flavour?” I said, thinking it was important. “Chocolate,” Uiluiit said. Uiluiit chuckled softly for a second or two, and then, with another breath, he looked up to catch my eye, and I could feel a subtle shift in the air between us. “But that’s not why I waited for you,” he said. “And you don’t need a ride,” I said, with a nod at the dinghy Gaba had rented. “I don’t.” I waited another few seconds, thinking that Arnet might have said something to Uiluiit, and that my break would soon be over because Uiluiit had given me a nugget of information that could change the nature of our babysitting operation. I just didn’t know why Uiluiit couldn’t have said it directly to Gaba when he had the chance. Or perhaps I had met one of the few male police officers in Greenland who was not under Sergeant Alatak’s spell. That in itself was interesting enough, but failed in comparison to what Uiluiit wanted to tell me. “You knew Constable Innaaq Paniula?” he said. “Yes.” I swallowed, and said nothing more, wondering just how much Uiluiit knew about what happened the last time I was in the area. The rumour mill among the Greenland police was an effective one, with gossip being a tradable commodity, especially for officers assigned to the more remote settlements where a lone constable might feel very isolated indeed. I understood that my exploits as a young constable had not gone unnoticed and didn’t doubt Uiluiit had heard a story or two, especially given that he was the local constable for the area. But he still surprised me when he told me what he had to say. “There is a cabin just off the path to Tasiusaq,” he said. “I was there about two months ago. Some tourists had taken shelter inside when one of them felt ill.” Uiluiit shrugged and said something about diabetes and helicopters, and a lot of paperwork. And then he looked me in the eye, took a breath, and said, “There is an old wooden desk in the cabin. Inside the desk is a drawer.” “Yes,” I said, aware that I needed to breathe once in a while, but too curious to risk losing a single word of what Uiluiit had to say. “Inside the drawer is a diary. It used to belong to Constable Paniula.” I nodded; eyes fixed on Uiluiit. “I only read a few lines,” he said. “But your name was on one of them.” “My name?” “Aap,” he said. “And you left it there?” “I was busy,” Uiluiit said, and I nodded. “Of course.” “But now…” Uiluiit pointed at the shore and the red and blue wooden houses of Qassiarsuk in the near distance. “Now you’re on a break.” “Yes,” I said. “Then I think you should go to the cabin, Constable. I think you should read Paniula’s diary.” “Yes,” I said, because I thought so too. The thought of catching a diamond smuggler – one of America’s Most Wanted criminals – had been interesting. And, while discovering the truth behind Rachael’s bruised cheek still occupied a tiny part of my mind, there was nothing, nothing that burned more insistently in my mind than the urge to get my hands on Paniula’s diary. “You’d better get going,” Uiluiit said. “The cabin is about halfway along the path. There and back is about seven kilometres.” “Yes,” I said, nodding once before pushing off the railing and heading for the dinghy. “I hope it’s worth it,” Uiluiit said as I climbed into the dinghy and fiddled with the outboard motor. I looked up and realised he knew that it was, and I guessed he had read more than just a few lines. “Good luck, Constable,” Uiluiit said, waving once as I started the motor. 
 5 There was a bit of spray splashing over the bow, but it had nothing to do with the wind, and the waves were of my own making. Gaba had said something about popping into Qassiarsuk to do the cultural thing and had suggested I take a couple of hours to do just that before returning to the ship to rest, and, I guessed, to grab something to eat before taking my watch. But I was already way ahead of him, dropping anything that might be confused as cultural, and plotting a brisk hike to the cabin. I figured I had just enough time to grab the diary, jog back to the dinghy, and sail back to the ship within three hours, leaving just enough time for a sandwich and a snooze before pounding caffeine in any shape or form I could get my hands on until the Americans arrived. It was a good plan. And, if I stuck to the plan, if I really focused on it, then I could stop my brain speculating on this or wondering about that, until I had the diary in my hands and discovered what it was Constable Uiluiit thought I might want to know. It could have been a coincidence, of course, but I thought it strange that, after all this time, Constable Innaaq Paniula should come back to haunt me. Which only made me think that I should really find out what happened to him. “Duneq,” I said, suddenly convinced that if anyone knew what had happened to Paniula, Sergeant Duneq would be the one. While I guessed I might sometimes be mentioned on the rumour mill, I wasn’t very good at keeping up to date with the latest rumours and gossip. “And neither am I going to get to the cabin and back at this rate,” I said, twisting the throttle for more power as I focused once more on getting the diary, not speculating about what might be written inside it. It’s a good plan. Stick to it. Qassiarsuk is a pretty settlement – not quite a village – with a perfect pebbly beach to land on. There are farmers’ fields positioned around the wooden houses, the store, and the utility buildings, and it always surprises me when I see plastic wrapped bales of hay dotted about a flat field, as if I was travelling through Europe, not bumping the bow of a rented dinghy onto a narrow beach in Southern Greenland. There was plenty to see in Qassiarsuk, and I promised myself that next time I would do the whole thing, that I would absorb every last morsel of culture and enjoy myself at the same time. Of course, it would be even more enjoyable with Atii, and I could almost hear her sigh as we stood in front of yet another informational sign, complete with dates and names and historical annotations. Yep, Atii would love it. Which only made me more determined to bring her along. “Diary first,” I said, wincing at the sound of the bottom of the dinghy’s hull scraping on the pebbles as I came in a little too fast. I ignored the passengers clumped in small groups on and above the beach and was oblivious to what emotions the sight of a police officer racing into the settlement might evoke among the older and more sensitive passengers among them. I was on a mission, and I was running out of time to get to the cabin and back to the ship. As much as I thought I might charm Gaba into forgiving me if I was a little late, neither did I want to chance it, especially when he was dealing with the Americans. Gaba often ratcheted up his game when working with foreign agencies, and I didn’t doubt he wanted everything to go smoothly. I did too. Which is why I almost forgot my manners when the first group of passengers stopped me just seconds after I had knotted the dinghy’s painter through a convenient iron ring bolted into a large boulder on the beach. “Are you here about the jewellery?” said a short, grey-haired woman with an ample waistline. She spoke in English, and I shook my head to jog myself out of mission mode and become a servant of the people again. Servant of the people. Yep, Atii would enjoy that one, and I made a mental note to never mention that I had thought the phrase into my head. “The what?” I said, slowing as the group enveloped me. “Jewellery,” the woman said. “We’ve all experienced it.” “I’m sorry? Experienced what, exactly?” “Strange jewellery in our pockets.” I curbed the urge to shake my head again and let out a quiet sigh, as I could just feel the time ticking away from me. “Have you had jewellery stolen from your pockets?” I said, thinking I had caught up. Greenland wasn’t known for its pickpockets, and there were hardly any people living in Qassiarsuk, let alone thieves skilled in the art of dipping their hands in tourists’ pockets. But that didn’t mean there weren’t thieves among the crew, and possibly even some light-fingered passengers onboard the ship. I sighed at the thought of spending more time dealing with petty crimes when all I really wanted to do was get to the cabin. “Not stolen,” said a tall man with a deep voice. “We’ve all discovered them.” “Discovered jewels?” I said. “That’s right,” the man said. “In our jacket pockets.” “The jackets you’re wearing?” I took a closer look at the red and yellow outdoor jackets the passengers wore. It was a uniform of sorts, identifying the passengers as belonging to the cruise ship. Different ships had different coloured jackets, but the effect was always the same – groups of typically grey-haired older people walking or shuffling around and through the settlements, or along gentle paths cut into the mountains to facilitate a smooth passage for the older generation of tourists. Like the path I’m supposed to be on. I suppressed another sigh, and pulled out my diary to make a show of professional sympathy, and took down their details, including the names of each member of the group who had discovered jewellery in their pockets, starting with Wilbur and Mary Franklin. “From Wisconsin,” Wilbur said. “We all are.” “Okay,” I said, scribbling Wisconsin beside Wilbur’s name. I stopped writing and did a quick mental calculation, wondering how quickly I could get to the cabin if I switched from a brisk walk out and a jog back to running both ways. I can still do it, but it’ll be tight. I took a breath and smiled at Wilbur. “Right,” I said. “Tell me about the jackets.” “And the jewellery,” Mary said. “Yes…” I nodded. “My mistake.” The light wind returned and tickled loose strands of my hair across my skin. I resisted the urge to look over my shoulder, as I knew the sight of white caps on tiny waves would require yet another recalculation as I wondered if it was still possible to get back to the ship on time. And then I relaxed, as I convinced myself I wouldn’t need a sandwich or a snooze after. And, honestly, who was I kidding? Did I really think I was going to sleep once I got my hands on Constable Paniula’s diary? Nope. It was highly improbable. Just as improbable as the idea of a Robin Hood pickpocket filling the pockets of well-heeled tourists with surprisingly expensive jewellery in Greenland. “Are those diamonds?” I asked when Mary showed me the ring she had found in her pocket. “Fake,” Wilbur said. “I’m sure of it.” I wasn’t. And if it wasn’t for Paniula’s diary, I just knew I would have been even more intrigued by diamond-studded jewellery turning up in the pockets of Dreamcaster’s passengers. But the wind was increasing in strength and the waves were growing bigger by the minute. I made a few more notes, took a few more names – also from Wisconsin – and then made a rather abrupt but hopefully professional exit, and headed for the path to Tasiusaq. I took a wrong turn up a sheep path, corrected, and then started to run. Time was running out, and the Americans were coming. 
 6 I’ve lost count of all the shifts I’ve worked with Atii when she drives and I run, but as I ran along the path, skirting around slow-moving clumps and clusters of red and yellow tourists, I owed her one. Sure, I was sweaty, and I realised I should have left my jacket in the dinghy, but I was really moving. Running while on patrol so often had also helped me refine the weight and balance of my utility belt. If I wasn’t so hot, I might even have enjoyed the streamlined feel of my belt with no unnecessary movement; I didn’t even have to press my hand on the grip of my holster, which was a first. The breeze helped keep my face cool, puffing small clouds of dust from the trail as I ran. I almost had enough excess energy to take in my surroundings – the bald granite peaks and tough green grasses that bent in the wind – but then I spotted the cabin, and it was all I could think of. I pushed on, vaguely aware that I had reached the halfway point between Qassiarsuk and Tasiusaq, and the two finger fjords on either side, and then took a hard left to jog down an uneven track to the cabin. It was, like many small cabins in the wilds of Greenland, in need of some serious, tender loving care. Flaps of bitumen on the roof lifted and clapped in the wind, and the walls were typically blistered from long summers of endless sunshine, drying and peeling the paint, followed by autumn rains and the deep, bone-chilling frost of winter to finish the job. I paused at the door, noted the frail hinges, and then lifted the handle up to open the door. Lifting the handle was supposed to deter polar bears, and it usually confounded more than a few tourists, but not the two elderly passengers sitting inside the cabin. They started as I barged in, and I caught that strange but wholly familiar sense of déjà vu as I recalled Uiluiit’s story about passengers in the cabin in need of evacuation. I’ll admit, given the time I had already wasted on the beach, I didn’t really want to waste any more time coordinating a rescue. Harsh, I know, but a quick look at the passengers revealed no immediate signs of distress. At least, no distress for them. My heart beat even faster than it had on the run along the path when I spotted the woman sitting on a rickety chair at the desk – the only pieces of furniture inside the cabin – as she delicately turned the mildewed pages of what could only be Constable Paniula’s diary. The man had his back to me as he studied the sheets of newspaper that had been stuck on the bare wooden walls like cheap wallpaper. I didn’t doubt the newspapers were old, and I was sure he was entertained, but he was also shocked at my abrupt entry, and, as they both looked up, I felt compelled to offer an explanation. “Hi,” I said, catching my breath and hoping to set them at ease with what had to be the most forced frivolity I had ever injected into my voice. Okay, frivolity and injected weren’t words I often used together, or, in the case of frivolity, ever, but I was on the clock and the woman had the diary I needed. “Hello,” the man said, while the woman simply stared at me. “I’m with the police,” I said, sticking to English. “So we can see,” the man said. “And, well…” I took a breath and pointed at the diary. “I need that,” I said. “It’s, ah…” “Evidence?” the man suggested. “Yes,” I said, taking another breath. “Joyce,” the man said. “Are you finished with the book?” “Yes,” Joyce said. She closed the diary and nodded. “I think so. I can’t read whatever language it is in, anyway.” She handed me the diary and said, “Is it important?” Paniula’s diary was heavy in my hands with a rough surface that seemed to prick my skin, letting the words seep through my fingers and into my body. I know how that must sound, but that was what it felt like, and the sensation was so strong, I didn’t hear what the woman said, and merely grunted in response. “I would take that as a yes, my love,” the man said, and I looked up. He caught my eye, smiled, and then made a shooing gesture at the door. “It’s all right, Officer. You look like you’re very busy. Joyce and I were just taking a breather before pushing on for the other village. The one that starts with a ‘T’.” “Tasiusaq,” I said, remembering my manners. “Yes, yes.” The man nodded. “The very same. We came on the cruise ship, you know.” “Yes,” I said. “Dreamcaster.” “The very same.” The man smiled and then turned to the woman. “Joyce, didn’t you say you saw the local police arrive onboard shortly before we left on this excursion?” “I did,” Joyce said. She gave me a stern look, and I guessed that I was unlikely to win her over, and if Atii had been there, it would have been up to her to charm the older woman into thinking I wasn’t really as rude as she might think. But, as I reminded myself, the clock was ticking. I had the diary, and it was time to go. “You’ve been very kind,” I said, pressing my palm on the cover of the diary and raising it slightly as if the pages contained weighty evidence that would make or break a case. “This will really help.” “I hope so,” Joyce said. “But don’t expect an easy read. Never mind that it’s in another language. The writer has scribbled all kinds of notes in the margins, and even between the lines. And then there’s the mould,” she said. “I recommend gloves, Officer, unless you want to catch something unpleasant.” I didn’t, and I thanked her for the tip before excusing myself and stepping outside. I opened the diary to check it really was Paniula’s, and then, seeing my name on the first page, I closed it just as quickly and slipped it into one of the larger pockets in my jacket. I checked the time on my smartphone and estimated that – even with the wind and waves against me – I could still get back to the ship in time to take a quick shower and maybe even borrow a shirt from the crew. I pressed my hand to my pocket and clutched the diary through the fabric. And then, taking a breath, I started to run. 
 7 I kept the diary dry inside my pocket for the choppy trip back to the cruise ship. The wind had shifted, and gave me a helpful shove from behind, giving me the chance to make up for lost time. I passed several Zodiac boats powering towards Qassiarsuk to pick up the passengers in stages and waved at each of the boat drivers on the way. The crew on duty guided me in alongside the floating dock with unnecessary but well-meaning gestures until they had secured the dinghy, and I turned the motor off. They mentioned something about a prolonged stay and wondered if they could secure the dinghy together with the Zodiacs when they removed the floating dock, and I nodded that they could. I didn’t think Gaba would object, and the casual mention of a prolonged stay suggested the crew were preparing to loiter in Qinngua for a little while longer. “But could I borrow a fresh shirt?” I asked, before climbing the ladder to the middle deck. “Ask in security,” the crewman said, and I nodded that I would. What I actually meant was I was wired. Paniula’s diary was quite literally burning a hole in the cargo pocket of my trousers, and I knew that dipping into it would keep me awake better than caffeine. Although I didn’t say no when Gaba said there was fresh coffee on the table opposite the cabins. I turned around to see Saarullik and Taateraaq rising from what looked like comfortable seats in an alcove with a bay window, one of many dotted along the length of the corridor. But they didn’t have Paniula’s diary, I thought, convincing myself it was the secret to staying awake while babysitting the American diamond smugglers. “There’s a rumour going around,” Gaba said as he pressed my MP5 into my hands. I followed him the few metres across the corridor and greedily reached for a sandwich when I spotted one. Gaba gave me the kind of look Atii did when she was convinced I was hiding something and then poured fresh coffee into two paper cups. “Thanks,” I said, wiping crumbs and mustard sauce from my mouth with the back of my hand before taking a cup from Gaba’s hand. “What’s going on, Constable?” he said, keeping it professional as I stuffed the last of the sandwich into my mouth and eyed the second. Gaba followed my gaze and nodded for me to take it. “Is this what happens when you catch up on a little Greenland culture?” “Yes,” I said, between bites and slurps of coffee. “Always.” “Right,” Gaba said. He fiddled with the sling of his MP5, adjusted it a little, and then glanced at the two Dreamcaster security officers strategically placed at either end of the row of four cabins. Sure, it was a reconstruction, but it was a good one, and I felt a tingle on my skin as we stepped inside. The interior was stone, wood, and reindeer fur, with pine supports that the original Vikings must have brought with them, for even back then, there were no trees in Greenland. The Inuit, my ancestors, had used driftwood for the frames of qajaqs and for other simple structures and tools, but the Vikings were the real artisans when it came to working with wood. “It’s your first time, isn’t it?” Rachael said as she watched me take it all in. “Yes.” And if I hadn’t felt the tingle on my skin, I might have picked up on what Rachael said, that it was my first time, but not hers. As it was, she told me a minute or so later, after I had gotten my fill of Viking heritage. “I was like you the first time,” she said. “Hell, I know it’s a reconstruction, but when you look at the village, it’s not a stretch to go back a couple hundred years and imagine how life must have been in the summer, before they all died that winter.” “You’ve been in Greenland before?” I said, still catching up. “Twice,” Rachael said. “And I bet that’s got you all razzled again, eh?” “Yes,” I said, aware that my so-called curious frown was in overdrive. “I came here with Sean,” Rachael said. “Of course, he was Barry back then, flying under the name of Barry August. He always said you needed something easy for an alias, to make it natural, easier to remember, and convincing. Well, I was convinced. About Sean, I mean.” Rachael wandered along the middle of the longhouse, towards a small modern table at the far end. I followed, content to let her keep going, as she pulled me into her story. “This was only a few years ago. We needed to get out of South America, and we wanted to go to Europe. But that didn’t quite work out, and we almost got ourselves pinned in London. We needed to take some time out, somewhere distant, and off the beaten track.” “Greenland,” I said. “That’s right, honey,” Rachael said. “You remember all those reasons you gave me about Greenland being the lousiest place in which to plan an escape? Well, you ain’t wrong, but if you’re not looking to escape, then everything you mentioned turns out to be just perfect when you want to lose yourself in plain sight. Right?” “I suppose so,” I said, frowning again as I tried to follow Rachael’s train of thought. “Of course, all this quiet, and all this nature with your big open skies, glaciers, and such… Well, it can be all kinds of inspirational, and Sean, dear Sean, was inspired.” Rachael stopped at the table at the end of the longhouse, put the MP5 down, and leafed through the pages of the guestbook, going backwards from the last entries, turning back time as she moved through the years. “Sean had this grand plan,” she said, stopping at one page and running the tip of her red nail down the entries. “He was still peeved about London. When the buyer pulled out, he was left with a tonne of hot diamonds that we couldn’t sell and couldn’t get out of the country. You can’t fly with a couple of million dollars’ worth of diamonds in your luggage.” Rachael looked at me and smiled. “I don’t suppose you’ve tried, honey? Have you?” She smiled again as I shook my head. “But what you can do is take them on a boat, especially if you pay top dollar. This is before they beefed up security on all the cruises. We chose the ones without the x-ray scanners for your luggage. They have them on most ships now, but the adventure cruises, back then, they were still taking off, and the kind of passengers booking them…” Rachael shrugged and said, “Let’s just say, they’re not exactly America’s Most Wanted, eh?” “I suppose not,” I said, thinking of the stereotypical cruise ship passenger with enough money to pay for a cruise to Greenland, usually at the end of their career, having worked hard to put enough money aside for the pension and some to spare for the fun stuff, like ticking things off the bucket list, Greenland included. “So, with a bag full of diamonds, and no buyer, Sean needed to get them into the States. He came up with this great idea and made some friends among the passengers. Some of them travel in groups, you know, usually friends from one town or state who’ve known each other for a couple of decades. Sean got to talking with them, told them he was in the jewellery business, and would they like to see some of the things he had with him?” “And they did,” I said. “Oh, yes.” Rachael laughed. “Especially the ladies. But more than one of the gents was impressed by the thought of wearing a diamond studded bracelet on their watch.” “And Sean gave them the jewellery?” “He let them borrow the jewellery. The idea was the diamonds were on loan for the duration of the voyage. And so he parted out the diamonds from the stash, with the idea that when these fine and innocent folk flew back to the States, a diamond ring with matching earrings in the luggage of one passenger, and a bracelet in the luggage of another, wouldn’t attract the attention of customs or those border patrol ruffians you often meet in America.” Rachael paused, and I guessed she was speaking from experience. “Now, Sean played it real cool. He never asked for any kind of insurance, didn’t take names or email addresses, but he made sure we were on all the excursions. And he made sure he was the first of our group to write in the guestbook, setting a precedent, you know?” “I think so,” I said, although I wasn’t sure. “He would joke when the passengers jostled him to hurry up. They’d tease him and ask if he was writing a novel or something? Tell him things like for gawd’s sake, Sean, it’s not poetry.” Rachael smiled and said, “I liked that one.” She flipped to another page in the guestbook and ran her finger down another column of names. “Another fellow said he thought Sean must be writing Pulitzer material, and that he was probably a journalist. But you know what Sean said?” Rachael turned to look at me, pupils dilated in the dim light. “He told them if a thing was worth doing it was worth doing well, and that after the fine folks in Greenland had taken the time to build such a captivating – he liked that word – reconstruction of a piece of important history, the very least he could do was print his damned name so it was legible, and tell them where he had come from, because they would surely like to know.” Rachael paused again, and I prompted her to continue with a nod. “But he wasn’t done. He told them they should at least put their mail address in the book, telling them some story about the Viking ancestors sending them a Christmas card each December, or some such rubbish. But they bought it, of course. And then, when Sean and me were gone from one day to the next, they had a few funny stories about that man who printed his name in all the guestbooks and left them with the most amazing jewellery that just had to be fake, because no sane man would ever leave real diamonds in the hands of strangers.” “Or pockets,” I whispered as Rachael turned her back on me and ripped one page after another out of the guestbook. She stuffed the pages into the inside pocket of her jacket and then picked up the MP5. “I wasn’t so sure about Sean being sane and I told him so when we jumped ship and flew to Copenhagen. He told me we’d catch up with our new friends once they got back to the States. And then, since they had been so kind to print their names and addresses in the guestbook, it would be easy enough to find them, retrieve the diamonds they had smuggled into America, and cash in.” Rachael sighed and said, “Only it didn’t work out that way.” “Because Sean didn’t have the guestbook, did he?” “No,” Rachael said. “That was my job. I was supposed to be last to sign the book. And then I was supposed to rip the page out when no one was looking. But I was young – too young to be discreet or even confident about that kind of thing, and, well…” Rachael shrugged. “So, you came back.” “Yeah,” she said. “Just a couple of years later.” Rachael looked up at the sound of a soft thumping noise that filtered through the turf roof of the longhouse. “Better late than never, I suppose,” she said. “Yes,” I said, although as the thumping noise grew louder, I wondered if time had run out for Rachael Silk and Sean Arnet, America’s Most Wanted. 
 13 I wanted to ask if Sean was doing the same thing again, only this time he didn’t bother to make friends, just dropped the jewellery into the passengers’ pockets, but the thumping sound was louder and even through the turf roof, the sound of a helicopter was unmistakable. “We should go,” I said, thinking that Rachael had said errands, plural, and that Gaba might have let her take me, so that I might see it through to the end. “Why?” “You can’t hear it?” I pointed at the roof. “That’s a helicopter. The Americans are coming, and you’re running out of time.” “That’s sweet,” Rachael said. “But you’re wrong, Petra. I have plenty of time. And if I need more, they’ll give it to me.” She shifted her grip on the MP5 and then nodded at the door, leaving me to guess whom she might be working for, or with whom she had struck a deal. Not Gaba, I thought. Although he had had plenty of time while I was on land chasing down Paniula’s diary. That thought stopped me cold, and I halted halfway down the length of the longhouse, oblivious to Rachael’s prodding and prompting, as I wondered if it was all a ruse, that Uiluiit had lied, or, worse, that Gaba had somehow set me up, knowing that I might be finished too quickly with a jag of Greenlandic culture, and return to the ship before he had finished making his deal with Rachael. “Then it’s a fake,” I whispered. “Something Uiluiit planted in the cabin and scribbled my name inside to make me think it really was the ramblings of a disgruntled and convicted police officer.” I pulled the diary out of my pocket and opened it to the first page. I ignored the thump of the helicopter and Rachael’s chiding as I found my name on the first page, holding my breath as I read the words around it, heart pounding as I found the names Paniula preferred to call me by, together with the name Venus Manumina, and that I was his Venus. Like father, like son, like… “I’ll take that,” Rachael said as she plucked the diary from my hands. I started to protest, but she simply raised the submachine gun and pointed the barrel at my chest. “I don’t know what you’ve got here, honey, but it’ll keep these pages flat,” she said, setting the diary down on the floor and crouching beside it as she pulled the pages of the guestbook out of her pocket and tucked them inside the diary. “There,” she said. Rachael slipped Paniula’s diary into her jacket pocket and stood up. “Give it back,” I said. I held out my hand. “Give it back or you can forget about me driving you anywhere else in the boat.” “Petra,” Rachael said. “You were doing so well, and now you’re getting razzled again.” She moved to one side to step around me, but I blocked her. “Give it back,” I said. “Honey?” Rachael shook her head. “This isn’t you. So emotional.” She took a step back, clacking her nails against the MP5 as she studied me. “What is it? Why is this book so important to you?” I couldn’t explain it if I tried. I had yet to read more than a few lines. But if the diary was genuine, and I thought it was too elaborate not to be, then it was a piece of my history, connected to a difficult episode in my past. Sure, we were standing in a reconstructed Viking longhouse, something from Greenland’s past. But it was so old, I could never really relate to it. The diary in Rachael’s pocket, however, was new. It was recent. And it was about me. “Petra,” Rachael said. She licked her lips as I took a step towards her. “You need to think about this, honey. You need to think real hard, now. Because…” She took a step back. “Because when I told you I never meant to hurt you, I meant it.” I took another step forward, and Rachael moved another step back. “You can’t get in my way, Constable,” she said. “I’ve come this far. I’m going to see this to the end.” “So am I,” I said, as Rachael flicked the fire selector switch on the submachine gun from safe to single shot. But I didn’t care, because, as I forced Rachael to take another step, and another, I remembered what Gaba had called me, and understood that even though he might have said lightweight, it was two words, not one. Light weight. But it wasn’t me Gaba was talking about, it was the gun. I thought it was lighter when he returned it to me, and I remembered the last time Atii had given me a light MP5, when she removed the bullets for fear of me pulling the trigger and killing a man when I really shouldn’t, no matter how much he might have deserved it. I didn’t want to kill Rachael. As far as I was concerned, she had done nothing to deserve it. Beyond taking a tight grip of my collar and jerking me around a bit, she had been as good as her word, hurting nothing more than my pride. But she crossed the line when she took Paniula’s diary, and ever since Uiluiit had told me about it, I had needed it. My colleagues knew me as the impulsive type, but Rachael Silk was about to discover my irrational side as I reached out for the MP5 and grabbed the barrel. “Honey, stop!” Rachael said. But I didn’t. I yanked the barrel, trusting that Gaba had replaced the magazine with an empty one, and trusting my interpretation of the words he whispered to me on the ship. Light. Weight. Sure, it was light. But Rachael was no lightweight, and she gave as good as she got, perhaps even better, as she tugged the submachine gun with masculine strength. Muscles that, provided she worked out, were always going to be stronger than mine. In the clash that followed, Rachael was a heavyweight, and we struggled for a few seconds, each tugging the gun, neither of us letting go, until a loud metallic click gave us both pause when Rachael pulled the trigger. “Oh, shit,” she said. “Oh, shit! Oh, shit! Oh, shit!” Rachael let go of the gun and stumbled backwards. She fell hard on the stone floor, bumping my pistol out of the back pocket of her jeans. It skittered across the floor, but she ignored it. Rachael continued to curse, waving me off as I tried to help her to her feet. “It’s okay,” I said, clipping the MP5 back onto the sling around my chest as I reached for her hand. “It’s okay. I’m still here. You didn’t shoot me, Rachael. I’m not hurt.” But Rachael was stuck in a moment. She couldn’t distance herself from the image of the barrel of the gun pointed at my chest and her finger around the trigger. “Rachael…” I took a step forward, but Rachael scurried to one side. She picked herself up and ran for the door. A shaft of early morning light pierced the longhouse as Rachael burst through the door, shining on my pistol on the floor. I grabbed it, holstered it, and then swore as I heard the helicopter thundering outside the longhouse, and then again when I was almost sure I heard the motors of the Zodiac growl. “Move,” I said, forcing myself out of the longhouse. “She’s still got the diary!” 
 14 There wasn’t just one helicopter, but two. I wondered if the longhouse reconstruction had included extra roof insulation, or if turf was just a more effective absorber of sound, but the sound of two helicopters was deafening as I burst out of the door and immediately threw my hands up to my face as a cloud of grit and sand and loose strands of hay engulfed me. It was what I’ve heard some helicopter pilots call a brownout, and I stumbled forward, unable to see more than a half a metre or less in front of my face. There were shapes and shadows, twists of something here and there. I might even have heard voices, but I wasn’t sure. I couldn’t smell anything either, as my nose clogged up with grit. I tried breathing through my mouth as I pushed my way through the cloud, turning my head to the right as I was sure I heard something. Maybe even Gaba’s voice, shouting for me to get down. “On the ground!” Not Gaba. He wouldn’t shout at me in English. “On the damn ground, lady!” And he would never call me a lady. And then, when two bulky shadows charged through the cloud and knocked me off my feet, I knew it wasn’t Gaba, and I guessed, from their voices and their actions, the Americans had arrived. It didn’t matter that my nose was stuffed and clogged. I was never going to be able to breathe with the American kneeling on my chest. “Get off her, now!” I heard the words but considering the lack of oxygen getting to my brain, it could have been a hallucination. As it turned out, it was Gaba. There was a scuffle, and I heard more shouting, more cursing, and the promise of wicked things happening to one man and then the other as a brawl broke out in the cloud of dust around the Viking longhouse. I rolled onto my belly and crawled away from the men fighting around me, barely aware that I had lost both my weapons for the second time in as many hours. But as I crawled, choking on gritty air, the helicopters settled in a farmer’s field to the left of the longhouse. The dust settled too, and I picked myself up, spitting grit and phlegm from my mouth, then wiping my lips with the back of my hand. I blinked, rubbed my eyes, and in the early morning light I saw icebergs in the fjord, and, working back to the shore, I saw the Zodiac I had borrowed still parked on the beach, and Rachael, still wearing her yellow jacket, bobbing about inside the boat. More heavily clad men spilled out of the helicopter and charged towards her. I played to my strengths and my light weight, and ran, determined to head them off. “Petra, wait!” Gaba again, but I didn’t look. I kept going, not slowing for a second. I saw Rachael climb over the side of the boat and push it into the water. The motors were still up, and I guessed the growling I had heard must have been Gaba’s boat. Rachael heaved, and the Zodiac slid deeper into the water, and she scrambled aboard as the boat bobbed, caught by the wind, and drifted into the brilliant, deep blue waters of Qinngua. “Constable!” I should have stopped, but something told me that if I did, something bad was going to happen to Rachael, and I picked up the pace, stripping away from the battle-ready men with their big guns, vests, and helmets, and racing onto the beach. “Don’t do it, honey,” Rachael said as I splashed into the water. “You have to stop. They’re going to shoot, Petra. Don’t…” Rachael ducked as the men fired the first warning shots above her head. They would aim at the boat next, with the intent to puncture and sink it. Unless they had already tried, and they are lousy shots. I might have giggled at that thought, or it might have been the effect of the freezing fjord water reaching my midriff. But when I lunged for the boat, I caught a grip on the safety lines looped along the sides. And then, after another volley of warning shots, Rachael reached over the side and grabbed my wrist. I kicked my feet as she hauled me over the side, until we were both sprawled on Zodiac’s deck, faces pressed to the ribbed metal surface as the men on the beach blasted the buoyancy tubes. Air hissed out of the tubes as they punctured, and Rachael laughed. “What’s so funny?” I said, shouting above the noise of the guns. “Nothing,” she said. “Oh, come on.” I reached for Rachael’s hand. “Don’t leave me in suspense.” “Okay,” Rachael said, following another laugh. “It sounds like I’ve got a bad case of gas.” She rolled her eyes and laughed again. And I joined her, just as another bullet burst another compartment of air. “So, Constable,” Rachael said. “What do we do now?” “First,” I said, pausing as the men on the beach were given the order to cease fire. “First, you need to know you didn’t hurt me. Okay?” “Okay.” Rachael nodded. “And second?” I shook my head and said, “I have no idea.” “What?” “No,” I said. “None.” “You mean, you ran through a storm of bullets, and dived into the frickin’ Arctic Ocean to get on a boat with more holes than a Swiss cheese, and you don’t have a plan?” “No,” I said, and sighed. “Jesus, honey, you are nuts.” “Yes,” I said. “I get that a lot.” I lifted my head – just a little – to peek over the rapidly deflating tubes, and glimpsed Gaba on the beach, hands on his hips, with Saarullik and Taateraaq on each side. Gaba stared straight at me, while the two constables had their backs to the water and their weapons casually pointing at a small group of heavily armed Americans on the beach. “Petra?” Gaba shouted my name from the beach. “Yes?” I lifted my head a little further and then stood up slowly. “The boat’s drifting, Constable. We’re coming to pick you up.” “Got it,” I said. Gaba paused for a second before shouting, “Are you okay?” “Yes.” “Both of you?” “We’re fine,” I said. I watched as another man wearing plain clothes, some might call bland, picked his way between the men on the beach to stand next to Gaba. He carried no weapons but had an impressive bullhorn in his right hand. He held it to his lips and pressed the button to project his voice across the fjord. “Rachael Silk? Can you hear me?” “Yes,” Rachael said as she stood up. “Do you have what we agreed on?” “Yes.” Rachael removed her jacket and held it over the side of the boat, soon to be a raft. I turned around and held my breath, suddenly aware of what she was threatening to do. “I’ve got it. Now, are you going to give me what you promised?” “Yes,” the man said. He lowered the bullhorn for a second as if he was collecting his thoughts and then pressed it to his lips again. “But you’re going to have to trust me, Rachael.” “I can’t do that, Barry.” Barry? There was something about that name. “But we had a deal,” Barry said. “Remember?” “I remember lots of deals. But I don’t remember ever getting what I wanted.” Rachael held the jacket out a little farther over the side. “Maybe it’s time to renegotiate?” “I can’t do that, Rachael,” Barry said. “It’s not an option. It’s non-negotiable, I’m afraid.” “Well, shit, Barry,” Rachael said. “Then I guess there’s nothing more to say.” Rachael tossed the jacket over the side of what was left of the boat, and I watched Paniula’s diary fly out of the pocket. The pages from the guestbook scattered in the wind as the diary slapped onto the water’s surface. “No!” I moved forward, shoving Rachael to one side as I leaped over the flat buoyancy tubes and dived into the water. “Petra!” I don’t know if it was Gaba who shouted. It might have been Rachael. But neither did I care as my fingers grasped the corner of the diary, and I clutched it to my chest as the cold cramped my fingers and I stroked, one handed, back to the sinking boat. “You are certifiable, girl,” Rachael said as she reached for me. “Yes,” I said, teeth chattering as she pulled me over the flat tube and onto the metal deck. “What the hell is so important about that book, anyway?” she said. “I don’t know.” I shivered for a few seconds, trying to speak. And then, as I saw Gaba in a Zodiac racing towards me, I looked at Rachael and said, “I haven’t read it yet.” 
 15 It took six duvets, four hours, and one electric blanket before I felt warm again. Gaba sat in the armchair at the end of the bed, removing grit from my MP5 with a cleaning kit he said he liberated from the Americans. He looked up from time to time, and every time I stirred, he looked at me. I caught his eye, but with my hands curled around the corner of the duvet, I kept my mouth and nose covered, hiding my smile as he watched over me. I would never tell Atii, but not doing something naughty with Gaba, was almost more exciting that doing what I sometimes fantasized about doing with the big, bald, macho leader of Greenland’s SRU. I know. Hopeless. But then, wasn’t it okay to be a hopeless romantic once in a while? “I know you’re awake, Petra,” Gaba said. “My eyes are open.” “Aap. But you’ve been awake for about two hours. Am I right?” I said nothing, preferring not to reveal that I had secretly watched him for almost as long as he had been watching me. He turned his head and nodded at the windowsill, and the bundle of towels within which I hoped I would find Paniula’s diary. “It’s ruined, of course,” he said, and I sighed. “The ink has run on most of the pages, but the deeper you get into the book…” “Yes?” I said, not daring to hope too much. “Well, it’s possible…” “Yes?” “I said it’s possible, Petra, that you might be able to read some of it. When it’s dried out, of course.” “Yes,” I said. “But before then, you’ll want to know about Rachael and the rest of her merry band of diamond smugglers.” “Her band?” “Aap,” Gaba said. “That’s what Barry says.” Gaba raised a thick finger to stop me from talking as he continued. “The three guys were what Barry called pastries, I think.” I giggled, and then pulled the covers down to say, “Patsies. Fall guys. Or dupes.” “Well, whatever they are, he said Rachael picked them up, and paid them a tonne of cash to pretend they were Sean Arnet and Co. She even paid them to stick the diamond jewellery in passengers’ pockets.” I was still processing the thought that there were three patsies, when I realised Gaba had moved on. “…confiscated as evidence, of course,” he said. “What was?” “The jewellery,” Gaba said. “Barry took it all as evidence, and he’s taking it all back to the States, along with Rachael and the three guys.” “It wasn’t fake, then?” “The jewellery?” Gaba shrugged. “Who knows, and who cares? We’re done with this one, Constable.” Gaba slid the MP5 and the cleaning kit onto the table and stood up. “Funny thing about Barry…” “Yes?” “He was a last-minute replacement. Apparently, the other guy who was supposed to lead the operation was sick with something. Barry just happened to be in Greenland, and stepped up, as they say.” “What was Barry’s last name?” Gaba shook his head and said, “I can’t remember. He probably told me. But the thing about him was there was nothing memorable about him. He had brown hair – a little thin, maybe. He wore boring clothes. Nothing stood out. Not even his accent. Everything about Barry was…” “Bland,” I said, cutting Gaba off. “Aap. That’s what I was going to say. “His name is Barry August,” I said, remembering what Rachael had told me in the longhouse. “He’s…” I sat up, suddenly warm and awake, only to grab the duvets again as I discovered I was naked. “Right,” Gaba said. “About that. You were cold, Petra. You were shivering. I had to get your wet clothes off you, and…” I gave Gaba a hard stare and then said, “And what about Saarullik and Taateraaq?” Gaba shook his head. “On the way back to Nuuk. We’re on the next flight, but you can take the ship a little further up the coast if you…” “Yes?” I said. Gaba held up his finger again, and I waited for him to catch on to what I said earlier. It was like watching the dawn break in the far north – a pale light growing stronger and sharper by the second. “What did you say the guy’s name was?” “Barry August.” “August as in…” “Sean Augustus Arnet,” I said, suddenly convinced that it was all starting to make sense. “The man who flew in as a replacement at the last minute and confiscated all the fake diamonds.” “Aap… And…” “Diamonds we think are fake.” “Sure, but all those men with guns, Petra. They were the real deal.” “The real deal who probably just made a hefty bonus on the side on an operation in a country most people have never thought about, or even heard of.” “So you think…” “Yes,” I said. I stood up slowly, covering my body with the bottom duvet, and wrapping it around me as Gaba’s brain was occupied with thoughts of how he had been duped, and might even be one of Sean Augustus Arnet’s pastries. Yes, I enjoyed that one. “But the commissioner…” Gaba said. “He talked to him.” “He talked to someone,” I said. “And we need to know who.” Gaba pulled out his phone and stepped out of the cabin, leaving me alone to peel back the towels and discover just how unreadable Paniula’s diary had become. Several of the pages were stuck together, and I didn’t dare peel them apart for fear of tearing them. But one of the pages was hanging out, and I tugged it free, only to realise it wasn’t a page from the diary, but something else that had been tucked inside. I turned around as Gaba burst back into the room, wearing a look I just knew could only mean trouble. “It’s him,” he said, clenching his fist around his phone. “It was August.” “Barry?” “Aap,” Gaba said. “He called the commissioner. He was the commissioner’s contact. We’ve been set up from the start. It was August’s idea to use Rachael. Can you believe that? He basically told me the play, and how to play it. He must have smuggled the diamonds onto the cruise ship, and then stepped off somewhere. He’s so bland he could have been anyone. But we’re not done…” “Gaba…” “This isn’t over, Petra. The commissioner is just as mad as I am. We’re going to get him. I have no idea how. But it’s a done deal. We’ll get him.” “Gaba, listen,” I said, as I plucked the extra page out of the diary. I waved it in front of him. “And what’s supposed to be?” “It’s what Rachael was going to use to negotiate a better deal with Sean. Or Barry.” I frowned and said, “I’m not sure. But whatever she wanted, he obviously wasn’t going to give it to her. And now…” “Now what?” Gaba said. “Now we’ve got he wants. You want to get him?” Gaba nodded. “Then this is how we do it.” “Right,” Gaba said. He reached for the MP5 and started putting it back together. “Gaba,” I said. “What?” “You’ve got a plane to catch.” He stopped what he was doing and then shook his head. “You mean we. Right?” “No,” I said with a nod at Paniula’s diary. “I have to catch up on my reading.” Gaba took a moment to take the hint, but I shooed him out of the cabin with the promise of delivering the page torn from the guestbook as soon as it was dry. But until then, I was going to try my very best to enjoy a Greenland cruise in the way it was supposed to be done. Slowly. Under the midnight sun. The End
